lesson.idea: Scan all 81 cells once and file each digit in three checklists: its row, its column, and its 3x3 box (box (r/3)*3 + c/3). A digit already filed means the board is invalid. Dots are skipped; the board is checked, never solved.
lesson.trap: The box index is (r/3)*3 + c/3: swapping the divisions files digits into the wrong box. Every digit needs all three lists checked, only non-dot cells count, and the first clash must stop the scan with false.
lesson.time: O(81) = O(1): the board size is fixed, so the single pass is constant work.
lesson.space: O(81) = O(1): three 9x9 flag tables (or three families of 9 small sets).
lesson.alt: Bit masks instead of flag tables: keep one 9-bit int per row, column, and box; test and set bit d for each digit. Same single pass and same O(1) bounds, but the whole checklist state fits in 27 integers.

lesson.idea: A permutation means equal 26-letter counts, so a fixed window of s1.length over s2 with a matches counter decides it.
lesson.trap: Rebuilding counts per window is O(26*n); comparing only at the end misses the early hit — update matches on entry and exit.
lesson.why: Sorting each window costs O(m log m) per step; two 26-slot count arrays plus a matches counter turn every slide into two O(1) count edits.
lesson.alt: Genuine alternative: sort s1 once and sort each s2 window of length m — same verdict, O((n-m)*m log m) time, O(m) space; fine for tiny inputs, too slow at 10^4.

pseudo.explain: GENERATE(n): top-level task — produce every well-formed string of n pairs, nothing else.
out ← []: accumulator for complete strings; the only collection that ever holds answers.
BACKTRACK(open=0, close=0, cur=""): recursive worker over the live prefix and its two counters, seeded empty.
if len(cur) = 2n: base case — the prefix consumed the whole budget, so it is a complete candidate.
append cur to out: record it; the guards guarantee every recorded string is balanced (no post-filter).
return: a complete string is a leaf — it has no children, so unwind one level.
if open < n: open guard — '(' may extend the prefix only while pairs remain.
Recurse on cur + "(": the open-first child; immutable strings mean no undo step is needed here.
if close < open: close guard — ')' may extend the prefix only while an unmatched '(' exists; this is the whole pruning rule.
Recurse on cur + ")": the close child; unreachable whenever the prefix is already balanced.
return out: after the root call finishes, out holds exactly the Catalan(n) well-formed strings.

lesson.idea: Backtrack over the live prefix with open/close counters: append ( while open<n, append ) while close<open, emit at length 2n; the close<=open<=n invariant makes every leaf valid.
lesson.trap: close<open, not close<n; undo the shared buffer in Java/C++ after each recursion; emit at len==2n, not open==n; order never matters.
lesson.time: O(n * 4^n / sqrt(n)): one O(n) copy per Catalan(n) leaf; n<=8.
lesson.space: O(n) recursion depth plus the output array.
lesson.alt: Closure-number recursion: split on the partner of the first ( as G(n)=union over c of ( + G(c) + ) + G(n-1-c); same output, cacheable subproblems. Brute-force enumeration of all 2^2n strings is the simpler cross-check oracle.

explain.explore: Recurse into the child call; it owns the appended bracket until it returns.
explain.record: Prefix reached length 2n, so it is complete and valid; snapshot it into the answer.
explain.unchoose: Undo the placement so siblings start from the same prefix; skipping this leaks characters across branches.
explain.return: Hand the full answer set to the caller; the working prefix is empty again at the top level.

lesson.idea: Hash map finds the node in O(1); a doubly-linked list with dummy head/tail keeps recency so get/put move the node to the front and eviction drops the tail.
lesson.trap: On a get/put hit you must unlink AND re-link the node (updating four pointers); on a full put you must delete the map entry for the evicted key, not just unlink it. Dummy head/tail remove all empty/single-node special cases.
lesson.alt: A LinkedHashMap (Java) or list+splice + unordered_map (C++) gives the same O(1) bounds with less pointer code, and a plain array scanned on every op is correct but O(capacity) per call — too slow for 2*10^5 calls. The explicit doubly-linked list is the portable interview answer because it shows the recency mechanics the question is really about.

explain.def: Declares the node shape and cache scope so pointer logic stays isolated from caller setup.
explain.init: Seeds an empty map with dummy head/tail linked together so every later splice has valid neighbours.
explain.lookup: Reads the map for the key without changing anything; the branch outcome is decided next.
explain.miss: Reports -1 for an absent key while leaving recency order untouched.
explain.hit: Moves the found node to the front and returns its stored value.
explain.update: Overwrites the stored value of an existing key and refreshes its recency.
explain.evict: Drops the tail (least-recently-used) node and deletes its map entry to free one slot.
explain.insert: Stores a new key at the front of both the map and the recency list.
explain.move: Unlinks a node then re-links it after the dummy head (used by hit and update paths).
explain.done: Closes the transcript; the recorded order and get results are final.

explain.init: Sets up the walkthrough scope and the preorder cursor so the first root read starts at the first element.
explain.map: Records each value once with its inorder position so the split point is found by lookup instead of search.
explain.call: Opens one bounded subrange call so left and right parts are solved independently and attached to their root.
explain.guard: Stops an empty subrange with null so missing children end without creating nodes or reading input.
explain.root: Reads the next preorder value in order and creates exactly one node for it, consuming one cursor step.
explain.lookup: Looks up the created value in the inorder map to split the range into left part and right part.
explain.recleft: Solves the left subrange next and attaches it as the left child so inorder left order is preserved.
explain.recright: Solves the right subrange next and attaches it as the right child so inorder right order is preserved.
explain.done: Returns the built subtree to its caller so the parent can attach it; the top call returns the whole tree.

lesson.idea: Preorder with one N marker per null child makes the token stream self-delimiting; a single shared cursor rebuilds the same structure.
lesson.trap: Skipping null markers misaligns the decoder: a chain needs a marker for every missing child or left/right swap silently.
lesson.alt: Level-order BFS codec writes one slot per heap position and rebuilds by index arithmetic; preorder is canonical for interviews because the cursor logic is shorter and works without heap math.

lesson.trap: Forgetting to clear the column/diagonal marks (or queens[row]) leaks an attack into sibling branches and silently drops solutions.

lesson.space: O(n^2) for the output boards plus O(n) recursion depth and mark arrays

lesson.idea: DFS from node 1 with a hash map from original value to clone node. The map is both the visited set and the wiring table: create the clone before recursing so cycles terminate, then fill each clone neighbor list with looked-up clones.
lesson.trap: Filling clone neighbors with ORIGINAL neighbors makes a shallow copy; checking visited without reusing the stored clone duplicates nodes on cycles; putting the node in the map AFTER the neighbor loop recurses forever on cycles.
lesson.time: O(V + E): each node is created once and each adjacency entry is read once.
lesson.space: O(V) for the map plus the recursion stack (O(V) deep on a line graph).
lesson.alt: Iterative BFS with a queue: seed clones[1], pop originals, and for each neighbor create-or-reuse its clone then link. Same O(V+E) with no recursion-depth risk; only the visit order changes.

java.text: public int coinChange(int[] coins, int amount) {
java.explain: Entry point: receives the coin set and the target amount; the table below derives from amount.
Sentinel scope: INF = amount+1 is worse than any reachable answer, so min() ignores it.
Table scope: dp[0..amount] will hold fewest-coin counts; every entry starts unset.
Base write: dp[0]=0 — the empty amount needs no coins.

java.text: for (int i = 1; i <= amount; i++) dp[i] = INF;
java.explain: Base fill: every positive amount starts INF (unreachable so far), never 0.
Amount scope: each i is solved left-to-right so every read hits an already-final cell.
Candidate scope: best tracks the minimum over the reachable predecessors for this amount.
Choice scope: try each denomination once per amount; order among coins never matters.

java.text: if (coin <= i && dp[i - coin] != INF) best = Math.min(best, dp[i - coin] + 1);
java.explain: Branch: only a fitting coin with a solved predecessor can improve best.

lesson.idea: Track the range [lo, hi] of possible open counts: '(' lifts both ends, ')' lowers both, '*' widens the range, and lo clamps at 0. Accept only when lo ends at 0.
lesson.trap: Fixing '*' to one meaning up front fails: '(*))' needs '*' as '(' while '(*()' needs '*' as empty. Keep the whole range, and clamp lo (not hi) at 0.
lesson.alt: Genuine alternative: two stacks holding indices of unmatched '(' and '*'. Sweep left to right pushing indices; on ')' match an open first else a star. Then match leftover opens against later stars in order. Same O(n) time, O(n) space, but the range version needs no storage.

pseudo.explain: Setup: widen n to 64 bits, flip sign once (reciprocal base, positive e), seed result at 1.

lesson.idea: Read the binary digits of |n|: square the base each step and fold it into result exactly on 1-bits. One sign flip up front handles negative n.

explain.def: Compute x raised to the power n with binary exponentiation: each 1-bit of |n| folds the current square into the answer.
explain.init: Normalize the sign once: a negative n flips x to 1/x and works with e=|n|, so the loop only sees e>=0.
explain.loop: Loop guard: each pass consumes one binary digit of e, so the loop runs exactly bitlen(e) times.
explain.compare: Read the lowest remaining bit of e: 1 means the current square is part of the answer, 0 means skip it.
explain.update: Fold the current square into result. Runs only on 1-bits; result is the product of the squares seen so far.
explain.square: Advance the place value: x becomes x^2 for the next bit, and e shifts right to expose it.
explain.done: e reached 0, every bit consumed; result holds x^n (already reciprocalized when n was negative).

Iterate i from 1 to n ascending so each dependency ans[i>>1] is final.
Apply the invariant ans[i]=ans[i>>1]+(i&1): halve-and-add-parity, then write ans[i].
Return ans: every position 0..n now holds the popcount of its index.

lesson.idea: Halving i drops its lowest bit, so ans[i] reuses ans[i>>1] plus (i&1).
lesson.trap: Do not recount bits per i; seed ans[0]=0. Non-negative n only per constraints.
lesson.invariant: After processing i, ans[k] = popcount(k) for all 0 <= k <= i.
lesson.mistake: Recomputing each popcount from scratch (O(n log n)) or forgetting ans[0]=0.

explain.init: Allocate the answer table ans[0..n]. It doubles as the DP memory: every later cell reads an earlier one.
explain.base: Seed ans[0]=0. Zero has no 1-bits, and every halving chain bottoms out here.
explain.loop: Sweep i from 1 to n exactly once, in increasing order, so ans[i>>1] is already final when read.
explain.update: Halving i drops its lowest bit, so popcount(i) = popcount(i>>1) + (i&1). One read, one write.
explain.done: Return the finished table. Its length is n+1 and every entry is final.

Guard: repeat exactly while a carry is pending.
Read + shift: the AND finds carry sources, the shift aims them at the next column.
Partial sum: XOR writes every resolved column into a.
Re-queue: the shifted carry is the next round’s work.

lesson.idea: XOR adds without carry; (a & b) << 1 is exactly the missing carry. Repeating both folds the carry in until nothing is pending (b == 0), so a is the sum.
lesson.trap: Loop on b != 0, not on a fixed count. Shifting the carry left is required — an unshifted (a & b) would re-add the same column forever. Negatives work because Java/C++ int arithmetic is 32-bit two’s complement.
lesson.time: O(1) — at most 32 carry rounds for 32-bit ints
lesson.alt: Recursive form getSum(a ^ b, (a & b) << 1) with base case b == 0 expresses the same invariant; an explicit mask loop ((a & b) != 0) is the same test written differently. Log-based or string tricks are not genuine alternatives here.

explain.loop: Loop while a carry is still pending; b == 0 means every column resolved.
explain.read: Read both operands at the same columns: AND finds the 1&1 positions that must carry.
explain.shift: Shift the AND left by one: a carry belongs to the next higher column, not its own.
explain.update: XOR writes the carry-free sum into a; the shifted carry becomes the new b. One read pair, two writes.
explain.done: b == 0, so a holds all columns including every propagated carry: return it.
